vignette:
He is a 53-year-old married man who has spent most of his adult life driving a bus, a job that once fit him well because it gave him a route, a routine, and a reason to keep moving. Before the trauma, he describes himself as steady, private, and capable of taking care of things without making a scene. He liked the predictability of his shifts, the familiar faces at the stops, and the simple rhythm of checking mirrors, opening the doors, and moving people safely from one place to another.

The assault happens in a way that leaves him feeling stripped of the world he thought he knew. He does not talk about it easily, but when he does, he describes the event with a flatness that seems to cover how much terror and shame are underneath. He remembers a sudden loss of control, the sense that his body is no longer his own, and the humiliating awareness that he cannot make it stop. In the days afterward, he is preoccupied with the belief that he should have fought harder or been able to prevent it. He feels dirty and exposed, and he begins to move through the world as if he is carrying something visible that other people can somehow sense.

At first he tries to return to work and to normal routines as quickly as possible, but that only makes him feel more raw. Sitting behind the wheel, he becomes acutely aware of who is getting on and off the bus, where they are standing, how close they come to him. He scans every passenger, especially men who resemble the assailant in build, voice, or scent. When someone stands too near the driver's seat, his shoulders tighten and his stomach drops before he has time to think. He keeps one hand ready at all times, as if preparedness alone might protect him. The bus, which used to feel like a contained and manageable space, begins to feel like a moving trap.

He starts taking different routes home if he can, avoiding the places that remind him of the assault. He stops going out at night unless he absolutely has to. Even in his own house, he is uncomfortable when doors are closed behind him. He checks locks repeatedly and has trouble settling in bed. Sleep becomes broken and tense. Some nights he wakes in a rush, disoriented and drenched in sweat, with the image of being pinned down or overpowered lingering long after he is fully awake. Other times he lies rigid beside his wife, staring into the dark, afraid that if he lets himself drift off he will be pulled back into the same helplessness.

He becomes more irritable and withdrawn, and his wife notices before he wants to admit it. He answers questions with short sentences and often seems somewhere else entirely. He avoids touch more than he can explain, even from the person he trusts most. Moments of tenderness now carry an undercurrent of alarm; a hand on his shoulder can make him flinch, and he is ashamed of that reaction because he does not want to hurt her feelings. He loves his family, but he feels separated from them, as if there is a glass wall between what they see and what he lives with internally. He thinks often about being a burden and hates how much effort it takes to appear "fine."

He also finds himself angry in ways that surprise him. Small frustrations at work or home can set off a wave of heat and tension that feels out of proportion to the moment. Then he is ashamed again. He does not like how much mental energy goes into staying controlled. At times he feels numb instead of angry, as if parts of him have gone quiet to protect against overwhelm. He says there are stretches of the day he gets through on autopilot, doing his route, speaking to passengers, stopping at lights, while some part of him remains braced for danger.

Over time, he develops a narrowed life organized around avoidance and vigilance. He keeps himself busy because stillness gives the memories room to surface. He notices that certain smells, tones of voice, or unexpected touches can bring the assault back with almost physical force. When that happens, he feels as if the present drops away and he is suddenly back in the original moment of powerlessness. Even now, he continues to work, but he does so with effort and caution, measuring each day by how much he can endure without breaking apart.
